l: Megara, The Library, force of Thracians.1 When Erechtheus inquired of
s: Megara received Pandion after he was expelled from Athens. Pylas gave its kingdom to Pandion before departing for Peloponnese, and Minos later captured Megara while Nisus was king.

l: Aegeus, The Library, force of Thracians.1 When Erechtheus inquired of
s: Aegeus was one of Pandion’s sons and held the whole power after the government was divided. He consulted the oracle about having children, visited Troezen, and lay with Aethra after Pittheus made him drunk. He left a sword and sandals under a rock for the male child Aethra might bear, then returned to Athens.

l: Nisus, The Library, force of Thracians.1 When Erechtheus inquired of
s: Nisus was one of Pandion’s sons and later ruled Megara. He had a purple hair in the middle of his head, and an oracle said that he would die if it were removed. His daughter Scylla pulled it out, and Nisus died through her treachery.

l: Troezen, The Library, force of Thracians.1 When Erechtheus inquired of
s: Troezen was the place through which Aegeus passed on his return to Athens. There he lodged with Pittheus and encountered Aethra.

l: Pittheus, The Library, force of Thracians.1 When Erechtheus inquired of
s: Pittheus, son of Pelops, hosted Aegeus at Troezen. After understanding the oracle, he made Aegeus drunk and caused him to lie with his daughter Aethra.

l: Aethra, The Library, force of Thracians.1 When Erechtheus inquired of
s: Aethra lay with Aegeus after Pittheus made him drunk, and Poseidon also had intercourse with her that night. Aegeus instructed her to raise any male child without saying whose child he was and to send him away with the sword and sandals once he could move the rock.

l: Theseus, The Library, force of Thracians.1 When Erechtheus inquired of
s: Theseus is identified in the accompanying notes with the male child whom Aethra was instructed to raise and later send away with Aegeus’s sword and sandals.

l: Panathenian festival, The Library, force of Thracians.1 When Erechtheus inquired of
s: The Panathenian games were held in Athens, and Androgeus won against all competitors.

l: Androgeus, The Library, force of Thracians.1 When Erechtheus inquired of
s: Androgeus, son of Minos, defeated all competitors at the Panathenian games. Aegeus sent him against the bull of Marathon, which killed him; another account says that jealous competitors ambushed and killed him while he was traveling to Thebes for the games in honor of Laius.

l: Minos, The Library, force of Thracians.1 When Erechtheus inquired of
s: When Minos learned of Androgeus’s death, he interrupted his sacrifice in Paros by throwing away his garland and stopping the flute, though he completed the sacrifice. He later attacked Athens, captured Megara, killed Megareus, and caused the Athenians to send seven youths and seven maidens to the Minotaur.

l: Scylla, The Library, force of Thracians.1 When Erechtheus inquired of
s: Scylla, daughter of Nisus, fell in love with Minos and pulled the purple hair from her father’s head, causing his death. After Minos captured Megara, he tied Scylla by the feet to the stern of his ship and drowned her.

l: famine, The Library, force of Thracians.1 When Erechtheus inquired of
s: Famine afflicted Athens during the prolonged war with Minos.

l: pestilence, The Library, force of Thracians.1 When Erechtheus inquired of
s: Pestilence afflicted Athens during the prolonged war with Minos.

l: daughters of Hyacinth, The Library, force of Thracians.1 When Erechtheus inquired of
s: The daughters of Hyacinth were Antheis, Aegleis, Lytaea, and Orthaea. They were slaughtered by the Athenians on the grave of Geraestus, the Cyclops, in accordance with an ancient oracle.

l: sacrifice of the daughters of Hyacinth, The Library, force of Thracians.1 When Erechtheus inquired of
s: The Athenians performed the sacrifice of the daughters of Hyacinth to seek relief from the famine and pestilence afflicting Athens. The sacrifice was of no benefit, so they consulted the oracle again.

l: Minotaur, The Library, force of Thracians.1 When Erechtheus inquired of
s: The Minotaur was confined in the Labyrinth and received seven Athenian youths and seven maidens as food.

l: seven Athenian youths and seven maidens, The Library, force of Thracians.1 When Erechtheus inquired of
s: The Athenians were ordered by Minos to send seven youths and an equal number of maidens without weapons as food for the Minotaur.

l: Labyrinth, The Library, force of Thracians.1 When Erechtheus inquired of
s: The Labyrinth confined the Minotaur. Its many winding turns prevented anyone who entered from finding the way out, and Daedalus constructed it.

l: Daedalus, The Library, force of Thracians.1 When Erechtheus inquired of
s: Daedalus, son of Eupalamus and Alcippe, was an excellent architect and the first inventor of images. He fled Athens after throwing his sister’s son Talos from the Acropolis, was condemned at the Areopagus, and fled to Minos; he constructed the Labyrinth and made a wooden cow for Pasiphae.

l: The Library, The Library, ΧΥ͂Ι. Θησεὺς δὲ γεννηθεὶς ἐξ Αἴθρας Αἰγεῖ
s: Theseus, son of Aegeus and Aethra, retrieves his sandals and sword from beneath a stone and travels on foot to Athens, clearing the road of criminals. He kills Periphetes and Sinis, taking Periphetes’ iron club for himself. Daedalus is tried in the Areopagus and, after being condemned, flees to Minos; he later helps Pasiphae approach Poseidon’s bull by making a wooden cow and constructs the labyrinth. The Athenians send seven youths and seven maidens each year to the labyrinth as food for the Minotaur.

l: Theseus, The Library, ΧΥ͂Ι. Θησεὺς δὲ γεννηθεὶς ἐξ Αἴθρας Αἰγεῖ
s: Theseus is born to Aegeus and Aethra. When he becomes mature, he removes a stone, retrieves his sandals and sword, and travels on foot to Athens, killing Periphetes and Sinis on the way; he takes Periphetes’ iron club and uses it himself.

l: Athens, The Library, ΧΥ͂Ι. Θησεὺς δὲ γεννηθεὶς ἐξ Αἴθρας Αἰγεῖ
s: Athens is Theseus’s destination. Its people send seven youths and seven maidens to the labyrinth every year as food for the Minotaur.

l: Daedalus, The Library, ΧΥ͂Ι. Θησεὺς δὲ γεννηθεὶς ἐξ Αἴθρας Αἰγεῖ
s: Daedalus’s corpse is discovered, and he is tried in the Areopagus. After being condemned, he flees to Minos; he helps Pasiphae by contriving a wooden cow and constructs the labyrinth.

l: Minos, The Library, ΧΥ͂Ι. Θησεὺς δὲ γεννηθεὶς ἐξ Αἴθρας Αἰγεῖ
s: Minos receives Daedalus after Daedalus flees following his condemnation.

l: Pasiphae, The Library, ΧΥ͂Ι. Θησεὺς δὲ γεννηθεὶς ἐξ Αἴθρας Αἰγεῖ
s: Pasiphae falls in love with the bull of Poseidon. Daedalus assists her by contriving a wooden cow.

l: Marathonian bull, The Library, ΧΥ͂Ι. Θησεὺς δὲ γεννηθεὶς ἐξ Αἴθρας Αἰγεῖ
s: The bull of Poseidon is loved by Pasiphae.

l: wooden cow, The Library, ΧΥ͂Ι. Θησεὺς δὲ γεννηθεὶς ἐξ Αἴθρας Αἰγεῖ
s: Daedalus contrives a wooden cow to assist Pasiphae after she falls in love with the bull of Poseidon.

l: Labyrinth, The Library, ΧΥ͂Ι. Θησεὺς δὲ γεννηθεὶς ἐξ Αἴθρας Αἰγεῖ
s: Daedalus constructs the labyrinth. The Athenians send seven youths and seven maidens there each year as food for the Minotaur.

l: Minotaur, The Library, ΧΥ͂Ι. Θησεὺς δὲ γεννηθεὶς ἐξ Αἴθρας Αἰγεῖ
s: The Minotaur is fed the seven youths and seven maidens whom the Athenians send to the labyrinth each year.

l: The Library, The Library, XVI. Aethra bore to Aegeus a son Theseus, and
s: Aethra bore Aegeus a son, Theseus, who grew up, moved a rock, took sandals and a sword, and traveled on foot to Athens. He cleared the road to Athens of evildoers. In Epidaurus, Theseus killed Periphetes and took his iron club. At the Isthmus of Corinth, Theseus killed Sinis, who forced passers-by to bend pine trees until they were tossed up and killed.

l: Aegeus, The Library, XVI. Aethra bore to Aegeus a son Theseus, and
s: Aegeus was the father of Theseus.

l: Theseus, The Library, XVI. Aethra bore to Aegeus a son Theseus, and
s: Theseus grew up, pushed away a rock, took the sandals and sword, and hastened on foot to Athens. He cleared the road of evildoers, killed Periphetes in Epidaurus, took Periphetes's iron club, and later killed Sinis.

l: Athens, The Library, XVI. Aethra bore to Aegeus a son Theseus, and
s: Athens was Theseus's destination as he traveled on foot.

l: road to Athens, The Library, XVI. Aethra bore to Aegeus a son Theseus, and
s: The road to Athens had been beset by evildoers. Theseus cleared it.

l: Epidaurus, The Library, XVI. Aethra bore to Aegeus a son Theseus, and
s: Epidaurus was the first place where Theseus killed an evildoer, Periphetes.

l: Periphetes, The Library, XVI. Aethra bore to Aegeus a son Theseus, and
s: Periphetes was the son of Hephaestus and Anticlia and was surnamed the Clubman. He was crazy on his legs and used an iron club to kill passers-by, but Theseus wrested the club from him and killed him.

l: iron club, The Library, XVI. Aethra bore to Aegeus a son Theseus, and
s: The iron club was carried by Periphetes, who used it to kill passers-by. Theseus wrested it from Periphetes and continued to carry it.

l: Sinis, The Library, XVI. Aethra bore to Aegeus a son Theseus, and
s: Sinis was the son of Polypemon and Sylea, daughter of Corinthus, and was surnamed the Pine-bender. He forced passers-by to bend pine trees, but Theseus killed him.

l: the Isthmus of Corinth, The Library, XVI. Aethra bore to Aegeus a son Theseus, and
s: The Isthmus of Corinth was where Sinis lived and forced passers-by to bend pine trees. Theseus killed Sinis there.

l: pine trees, The Library, XVI. Aethra bore to Aegeus a son Theseus, and
s: Sinis forced passers-by to keep bending pine trees. The passers-by were too weak to do so and were tossed up by the trees, perishing miserably.

l: The Library, The Library, APOLLODORI BIBLIOTHECA
s: Theseus killed the sow called Phaia at Crommyon; Phaia was named after the old woman who raised it, though some identified it as a child of Echidna and Typhon. Theseus then killed Sciron, described as a Corinthian and, according to differing accounts, either a son of Pelops or of Poseidon. Sciron forced travelers at the Scironian Rocks to wash his feet before throwing them into the depths as food for an enormous turtle, but Theseus seized him by the feet and threw him into the sea.

l: Theseus, The Library, APOLLODORI BIBLIOTHECA
s: Theseus killed Phaia at Crommyon. He also seized Sciron by the feet and threw him into the sea.

l: Phaia, The Library, APOLLODORI BIBLIOTHECA
s: Phaia was a sow killed by Theseus at Crommyon. She was named after the old woman who raised her; some said she was a child of Echidna and Typhon.

l: Sciron, The Library, APOLLODORI BIBLIOTHECA
s: Sciron was a Corinthian who was described as a son of Pelops, though some said he was a son of Poseidon. At the Scironian Rocks in the Megaric region, he forced passersby to wash his feet and then threw them into the depths as food for an enormous turtle; Theseus seized him by the feet and threw him into the sea.

l: Theseus's killing of Phaia, The Library, APOLLODORI BIBLIOTHECA
s: Theseus's killing of Phaia occurred at Crommyon, where he killed the sow called Phaia.

l: Theseus's killing of Sciron, The Library, APOLLODORI BIBLIOTHECA
s: Theseus's killing of Sciron occurred when Theseus seized Sciron by the feet and threw him into the sea.

l: The Library, The Library, front matter
s: Theseus clears the road to Athens, survives Medea’s attempt to poison him, and is recognized by Aegeus as his son. He joins the third tribute sent to the Minotaur, enters the Labyrinth with Ariadne’s help, kills the Minotaur, and escapes with Ariadne and the rescued children. Dionysus carries Ariadne to Lemnos, while Theseus forgets to change the ship’s black sail, causing Aegeus to believe that Theseus has died and to kill himself. Theseus then takes control of Athens, and Minos imprisons Daedalus and Icarus in the Labyrinth until Daedalus makes wings for their escape.

l: Theseus, The Library, front matter
s: Theseus kills Sciron, Cercyon, Damastes, the Marathonian bull, and the Minotaur. He is recognized by Aegeus as his son, escapes the Labyrinth with Ariadne’s clue of thread, and later succeeds to the sovereignty of Athens, killing the sons of Pallas and others who oppose him.

l: Medea, The Library, front matter
s: Medea, then living with Aegeus, plots against Theseus and persuades Aegeus to regard him as a traitor. After Theseus is recognized by Aegeus, Medea is expelled.

l: Aegeus, The Library, front matter
s: Aegeus does not initially know that Theseus is his son and sends him against the Marathonian bull. He receives a sword from Theseus, recognizes him, and knocks the poisoned cup from Theseus’s hands; later, seeing the ship’s black sail, he believes Theseus has died and kills himself.

l: Marathonian bull, The Library, front matter
s: The Marathonian bull is sent against Theseus by Aegeus, and Theseus kills it.

l: Athens, The Library, front matter
s: Theseus reaches Athens after clearing the road and later takes control of the city’s government.

l: Minotaur, The Library, front matter
s: The Minotaur receives the third tribute, into which Theseus is included. Theseus finds and kills it in the innermost part of the Labyrinth.

l: Cretan tribute, The Library, front matter
s: The Cretan tribute includes Theseus as part of the third group sent to the Minotaur. Some say that Theseus volunteered for it.

l: ship of Theseus, The Library, front matter
s: The ship carries Theseus, Ariadne, and the rescued children from Crete toward Athens. Theseus forgets to change its black sail, leading Aegeus to believe that he has died.

l: black sail, The Library, front matter
s: The ship of Theseus has a black sail when it returns. Aegeus sees it from the acropolis and, believing Theseus has perished, kills himself.

l: white sails, The Library, front matter
s: Aegeus instructs Theseus to spread white sails if he returns alive. Theseus forgets to do so because he is grieving over Ariadne.

l: Ariadne, The Library, front matter
s: Ariadne, daughter of Minos, falls in love with Theseus and offers to help him if he promises to take her to Athens as his wife. She obtains from Daedalus the means of finding the Labyrinth’s exit, leaves Crete with Theseus, and is later carried off by Dionysus to Lemnos.

l: Minos, The Library, front matter
s: Minos has the Minotaur in the Labyrinth and, after learning that those with Theseus have escaped, imprisons Daedalus and Icarus in the Labyrinth.

l: Daedalus, The Library, front matter
s: Daedalus discloses the way out of the Labyrinth at Ariadne’s request and provides the plan for using a clue of thread. Minos later imprisons him in the Labyrinth with Icarus, after which Daedalus makes wings for himself and Icarus.

l: Labyrinth, The Library, front matter
s: The Labyrinth contains the Minotaur and has an exit whose route Daedalus reveals to Ariadne. Theseus enters it with the clue of thread, kills the Minotaur, and follows the thread back out; Minos later imprisons Daedalus and Icarus there.

l: clue of thread, The Library, front matter
s: Ariadne gives Theseus a clue of thread following Daedalus’s advice. Theseus fastens it to the door, unwinds it as he enters the Labyrinth, and uses it to find his way out after killing the Minotaur.

l: Naxos, The Library, front matter
s: Theseus reaches Naxos at night with Ariadne and the children rescued from the Minotaur. Dionysus carries Ariadne away from there.

l: Dionysus, The Library, front matter
s: Dionysus falls in love with Ariadne, carries her off, and takes her to Lemnos, where he has children with her.

l: The Library, The Library, On being apprized of the flight of Theseus and
s: After learning of the flight of Theseus and his company, Minos imprisoned Daedalus and Icarus in the labyrinth. Daedalus made wings for himself and Icarus, but Icarus flew too high, fell into the Icarian Sea, and died, while Daedalus reached Camicus in Sicily. Minos pursued Daedalus by carrying a spiral shell and offering a reward to anyone who could pass a thread through it. Daedalus solved the challenge with an ant, revealing his presence to Minos; Cocalus then sheltered Daedalus, and Minos was killed with boiling pitch.

l: Theseus, The Library, On being apprized of the flight of Theseus and
s: Theseus's flight and that of his company led Minos to imprison Daedalus and Icarus in the labyrinth.

l: Minos, The Library, On being apprized of the flight of Theseus and
s: Minos imprisoned Daedalus and Icarus after learning of Theseus's flight. He pursued Daedalus with a spiral shell, discovered that Daedalus was concealed with Cocalus, and was killed when the daughters of Cocalus poured boiling pitch over him.

l: Daedalus, The Library, On being apprized of the flight of Theseus and
s: Daedalus was imprisoned with Icarus in the labyrinth, escaped by making wings, and reached Camicus in Sicily. He devised a way to pass a thread through a spiral shell, thereby revealing his presence to Minos.

l: Icarus, The Library, On being apprized of the flight of Theseus and
s: Icarus escaped the labyrinth with Daedalus using wings. He ignored Daedalus's warning, flew too high, and fell into the sea when the glue holding his wings melted.

l: Cocalus, The Library, On being apprized of the flight of Theseus and
s: Cocalus sheltered Daedalus at Camicus. He received Minos, promised to surrender Daedalus, and then allowed the daughters of Cocalus to kill Minos with boiling pitch.

l: Labyrinth, The Library, On being apprized of the flight of Theseus and
s: The labyrinth was the place where Minos imprisoned Daedalus and Icarus.

l: Camicus, The Library, On being apprized of the flight of Theseus and
s: Camicus in Sicily was the place where Daedalus was concealed with Cocalus and where Minos came in pursuit of him.

l: Icarian Sea, The Library, On being apprized of the flight of Theseus and
s: The sea into which Icarus fell was called the Icarian Sea after him.

l: flight of Theseus and his company, The Library, On being apprized of the flight of Theseus and
s: The flight of Theseus and his company caused Minos to imprison Daedalus and Icarus in the labyrinth.

l: Daedalus and Icarus’s flight, The Library, On being apprized of the flight of Theseus and
s: Daedalus and Icarus escaped from the labyrinth by flying with wings made by Daedalus. Daedalus reached Camicus safely, but Icarus fell into the sea.

l: Icarus’s fall and death, The Library, On being apprized of the flight of Theseus and
s: Icarus's fall occurred after he disregarded Daedalus's injunction and flew too high. The glue melted in the sun, his wings fell apart, and he perished in the sea that was called the Icarian Sea.

l: wings of Daedalus, The Library, On being apprized of the flight of Theseus and
s: Daedalus constructed wings for himself and Icarus. He warned Icarus not to fly too high, lest the glue melt in the sun, or too near the sea, lest damp detach the pinions.

l: spiral shell, The Library, On being apprized of the flight of Theseus and
s: Minos carried a spiral shell through the countries he searched and offered a great reward to anyone who could pass a thread through it. The shell enabled Minos to discover that Daedalus was with Cocalus.

l: thread, The Library, On being apprized of the flight of Theseus and
s: Daedalus fastened a thread to an ant and allowed it to pass through a hole bored in the spiral shell. Minos found the thread passed through the shell and inferred that Daedalus was concealed with Cocalus.

l: Minos’s pursuit of Daedalus, The Library, On being apprized of the flight of Theseus and
s: Minos pursued Daedalus through different countries, using the spiral-shell challenge to locate him. The pursuit brought Minos to Camicus, where he identified Daedalus's hiding place and was killed.

l: Cocalus’s ruse with the shell, The Library, On being apprized of the flight of Theseus and
s: Cocalus received the spiral shell from Minos after promising to thread it and gave it to Daedalus. Daedalus used an ant and a thread to pass through the shell, but the completed task allowed Minos to identify Daedalus's presence.

l: Minos’s death, The Library, On being apprized of the flight of Theseus and
s: Minos's death occurred at Cocalus's court after Cocalus promised to surrender Daedalus and entertained him. The daughters of Cocalus killed Minos by pouring boiling pitch over him while he bathed.

l: boiling pitch, The Library, On being apprized of the flight of Theseus and
s: Boiling pitch was poured over Minos by the daughters of Cocalus while he bathed, and it killed him.

l: The Library, The Library, ES 16
s: The unit recounts Theseus’s conflict with the Amazons, his marriage to Phaedra, and the death of Hippolytus after Phaedra’s false accusation. It also describes Ixion’s punishment by Zeus and the birth of Centaurus from the cloud resembling Hera. Finally, it recounts the wedding conflict of Pirithous, Theseus’s battle with the centaurs, and Caeneus’s burial beneath fir trees.

l: Theseus, The Library, ES 16
s: Theseus joined Hercules in an expedition against the Amazons and carried off Antiope, or, according to some, Melanippe; Simonides called her Hippolyte. He later defeated the Amazons near the Areopagus with the Athenians, married Phaedra, and had Acamas and Demophon by her. He believed Phaedra’s accusation against Hippolytus, prayed to Poseidon for Hippolytus’s death, and fought the centaurs alongside Pirithous.

l: Amazons, The Library, ES 16
s: The Amazons fought alongside Hercules against Theseus, and Theseus carried off Antiope, or alternatively Melanippe. They later marched against Athens, encamped near the Areopagus, and were defeated by Theseus and the Athenians. The Amazon previously married to Theseus appeared armed with other Amazons during Phaedra’s wedding and was killed, according to one account, after the guests shut the doors.

l: Antiope, The Library, ES 16
s: Theseus carried off Antiope during the expedition against the Amazons. Some accounts instead call the woman Melanippe, while Simonides calls her Hippolyte.

l: Athens, The Library, ES 16
s: Athens was attacked by the Amazons, who encamped near the Areopagus. The Athenians, led by Theseus, defeated them.

l: Phaedra, The Library, ES 16
s: Phaedra, daughter of Minos, married Theseus and bore him Acamas and Demophon. She fell in love with Hippolytus, sought intercourse with him, and falsely accused him of assault after he rejected her. When her passion became public, she hanged herself.

l: Hippolytus, The Library, ES 16
s: Hippolytus was the son of Theseus and the Amazon. He rejected Phaedra’s advances because he hated all women, and he was later dragged to death after Poseidon sent a bull from the surf and frightened his horses.

l: false accusation against Hippolytus, The Library, ES 16
s: Phaedra made a false accusation against Hippolytus after fearing that he would report her advances to Theseus. She tore open the doors of her chamber and her clothing to support the accusation, and Theseus believed her.

l: Poseidon, The Library, ES 16
s: Poseidon answered Theseus’s prayer that Hippolytus should perish. He sent a bull from the surf, frightening Hippolytus’s horses and causing the chariot to break apart.

l: death of Hippolytus, The Library, ES 16
s: Hippolytus died after his horses were frightened by a bull sent from the sea. His chariot was dashed to pieces, and he was dragged to death after becoming entangled in the reins.

l: Ixion, The Library, ES 16
s: Ixion fell in love with Hera and attempted to force her. After Zeus tested him with a cloud resembling Hera, Ixion boasted that he had possessed Hera and was bound to a wheel, where winds carried him through the air as punishment.

l: Hera, The Library, ES 16
s: Ixion fell in love with Hera and attempted to force her. Hera reported the matter to Zeus, who made a cloud in her likeness to test whether Ixion’s boast was true.

l: Zeus, The Library, ES 16
s: Zeus made a cloud resembling Hera to test Ixion’s claim that he had possessed her. After Ixion boasted about the encounter, Zeus bound him to a wheel and caused him to be carried through the air by winds.

l: wheel, The Library, ES 16
s: The wheel was the instrument of Ixion’s punishment. Ixion was bound to it and carried through the air by winds.

l: Pirithous, The Library, ES 16
s: Pirithous wooed Hippodamia and feasted the centaurs because they were her kinsmen. When the drunken centaurs attempted to violate the bride, Pirithous armed himself and fought them with Theseus.

l: centaurs, The Library, ES 16
s: The centaurs were invited to the wedding of Pirithous because they were related to Hippodamia. After drinking excessively, they attempted to violate the bride, and many were killed in the battle with Pirithous and Theseus.

l: wedding of Pirithous, The Library, ES 16
s: At the wedding of Pirithous and Hippodamia, the centaurs were feasted as her kinsmen. They became drunk and attempted to violate the bride, leading Pirithous and Theseus to fight them.

l: Caeneus, The Library, ES 16
s: Caeneus had formerly been a woman, but after intercourse with Poseidon he asked to become an invulnerable man. During the battle with the centaurs, he killed many of them while disregarding wounds, but the remaining centaurs surrounded him and buried him in the earth by striking him with fir trees.

l: battle between the Lapiths and centaurs, The Library, ES 16
s: The battle occurred at the wedding of Pirithous and Hippodamia after the centaurs attempted to violate the bride. Pirithous and Theseus fought the centaurs, and Theseus killed many of them.

l: The Library, The Library, 23 Ὅτι Θησεύς, Πειρίθῳ συνθέμενος Διὸς θυ-
s: Theseus and Pirithous agreed to marry daughters of Zeus. Theseus abducted Helen from Sparta, while Pirithous sought Persephone and descended with Theseus into Hades. The Dioscuri captured Athens, carried away Helen and Aethra, and brought Menestheus back to rule Athens. In Hades, Theseus and Pirithous were deceived and bound to the Chair of Forgetfulness; Heracles rescued Theseus, who was later driven from Athens by Menestheus.

l: Theseus, The Library, 23 Ὅτι Θησεύς, Πειρίθῳ συνθέμενος Διὸς θυ-
s: Theseus agreed with Pirithous to marry daughters of Zeus and abducted Helen from Sparta. He descended with Pirithous into Hades, where he was deceived and bound to the Chair of Forgetfulness. Heracles brought him back and sent him to Athens, but Menestheus later drove him out.

l: Pirithous, The Library, 23 Ὅτι Θησεύς, Πειρίθῳ συνθέμενος Διὸς θυ-
s: Pirithous agreed with Theseus to marry daughters of Zeus and helped Theseus abduct Helen. He descended with Theseus into Hades in pursuit of marriage with Persephone and was bound there forever.

l: Helen, The Library, 23 Ὅτι Θησεύς, Πειρίθῳ συνθέμενος Διὸς θυ-
s: Helen was abducted from Sparta by Theseus with the help of Pirithous when she was twelve years old. The Dioscuri later carried her away from Athens.

l: abduction of Helen, The Library, 23 Ὅτι Θησεύς, Πειρίθῳ συνθέμενος Διὸς θυ-
s: Theseus and Pirithous abducted Helen from Sparta for Theseus when she was twelve years old. The Dioscuri later carried Helen away with Aethra.
